He had brought a card, cream-colored and edged in gilt, inviting her family to his sister's wedding. Takeshi read it, set it beside the scales, and said she could not leave the shop on a Saturday. She had closed the shop for lesser reasons, and he had guessed her answer before he ever crossed the street; yet he lingered, praising the loaves as though they were the reason for his visit. g.passage: When the last students had filed out of the classroom, I found Jomo still at the back desk, turning an old photograph over in his fingers. I had borrowed the room from the language school because our pitch was flooded, and the whiteboard still listed French verbs in someone else's tidy hand. The photograph showed our team two seasons ago, Jomo lifted on his teammates' shoulders, his mouth open in a shout. He asked whether I remembered that match. I said I did, which was true, and that it had nothing to do with Saturday's lineup, which was also true. Even so, I could not stop looking at the boy in the picture, and I envied him a little for being so certain of what he was owed. Outside, a minibus honked twice in the Addis Ababa traffic, and the rain eased into a thin, warm drizzle.

g.passage:
Shanghai wakes late in this lane of kilns,
and I arrive before the studio doors are open.
Jiayi, who farmed rice until the city reached her,
shapes a bowl as if she is patting soil flat.
Her daughter Ruoxi, home from surveying new roads,
measures the shelf with her eyes and calls it crowded.
They argue about price, about glaze, about space.
Neither notices how every bowl leans the same way,
a small tilt toward the window, like seedlings
looking for weather. I do not tell them.
Some knowledge belongs to the hands that made it,
and a guest should carry her cup carefully.
On the tram back, a man sells chestnuts from a tin,
and the steam fogs the glass in quick white circles.

g.passage: By my third winter in Riga, I knew the stairwell of my building better than my own kitchen: the cracked fourth step, the radiator that knocked like a guest. Jiwoo, who drove the bus I took each morning, lived two floors below. One evening I found her sitting on the landing beside Beatriz, the widow from the top floor, who had forgotten her keys again and had been weeping. Jiwoo held a finger to her lips when she saw me. The next morning on the bus, she said nothing about it, and neither did I, though we had talked about everything else for years: snow, fares, her son's exams. I used to think silence between friends meant distance. Now I count that quiet among the few promises I have kept well. On Saturdays the stairwell smells of cabbage and floor wax, and someone on the second floor practices scales on an out-of-tune piano.

g.passage: What do you say to someone who left without a word and comes back the same way? I asked myself that at the bus depot in Gdansk, where my brother Marcus and I had gone to meet Zofia, our cousin, eleven years after she boarded a coach to Berlin. Marcus had polished his shoes; I had not. Our shop sold fewer radios each month, and he talked about it on the drive as if Zofia might bring customers in her suitcase. She stepped down carrying one small bag and kissed us both, and she explained nothing. I waited for an apology that never came and was surprised to find I did not need it. Watching her laugh at Marcus's terrible jokes, I thought the years had cost her more than they had cost us. A cleaner moved between the empty bays, pushing a wide broom over oil stains shaped like countries.

g.passage:
Anacleto,
I am writing from the projection booth, where the old machine still smells of oil and dust even though no film has run through it since spring. Your father's plane arrived this morning, wrapped in a flour sack, with a note saying he wished me to have it. I know you expected it. You swept his shop for six years before I ever held a chisel, and I have seen you run your thumb along that blade as if greeting someone. I will use it, because refusing a dead man's gift seems worse than accepting it badly. But every board I smooth will be a board I owe you, and I mean to keep the account. Tell your mother the booth's door finally closes; I rehung it on Tuesday with new hinges.
Cleotilde

Emil thanked him warmly and wore them to stir the porridge, though his knuckles pressed white against the seams. g.passage: "Same as always?" Shamsuddin asked, and Danish nodded, which was most of their conversation for the afternoon. Every Thursday for forty years, the two men had come back to the music room of the Karachi school where they had once been students, to tune its tired harmonium and dust the tabla skins. Neither was paid. Neither, as far as I ever saw, suggested stopping. As a boy I sat on the bench and watched them work, my grandfather pressing keys while his friend adjusted reeds, and I thought them dull. Only later did I notice how each corrected note seemed to answer the one before, like a sentence the other could finish. When Danish died, Shamsuddin came the next Thursday alone and tuned the instrument to the same pitch. Afterward the room was locked, and the key hung on a nail in the headmaster's office.

g.passage:
Dear Fumiko,
I lost again. You will be pleased, though you will pretend otherwise when we meet at the club. I am writing from a train compartment somewhere in Hokkaido, with our travel set balanced on my knees, replaying the endgame you won on Sunday. For twelve years we have played every week, and for twelve years neither of us has mentioned the tournament in Osaka or the move you swear you did not take back. I used to think our silence was cowardice. Lately I suspect it is the only reason we still sit across from each other. The snow here has buried the fences entirely; only the tops of the telegraph poles mark the road.
Yours in rivalry,
Rukhsana

g.passage: Years ago, on the promenade by the Lagos sea, a nephew named Casey owed his uncle Babatunde the price of a fishing boat. Each evening Casey walked the seawall with coins in his pocket, meaning to pay, and each evening he bought roasted corn instead and told himself tomorrow. Babatunde saw this from his bench and said nothing. When at last Casey came with the full amount, the old man counted it twice, then pressed half of it back into his hand.
